name: Ben Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Ben. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a grader at a bauxite mine, keeping the haul roads smooth so the trucks don't wreck their tyres. Twelve-hour shifts, mostly days. For twenty-five years I ran the family hardware shop on Main Street, which my father opened, until a big chain store opened on the highway and took our customers. That's the market, no hard feelings. At fifty-five I sold the stock, and a mate from church got me in here.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still not great. The road boss, Kerry, says I leave the crown too flat and water pools in the middle. But I enjoy it, and I've got a habit of asking the AI on my phone every night what I did wrong. I used it to do the shop's books in the last few years, and now I use it for everything, from grader angles to reading the company's annual report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, the market's decided it's a useful tool and not a miracle. I'd post a short note about it on the business forum I still read. At work I'd just keep grading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the tools and I'd been half planning around them. But it means a steady run to retirement, which suits Lin and me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading, keep learning, and get Kerry off my back about the crown by next winter. I'd keep using AI daily for the job and for our small share portfolio. And I'd keep saving a few hundred a month, because the shop sale didn't leave us much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A shrug, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the shop sale leave you with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After paying the suppliers, about four months of living costs, plus a small super balance that never got much love while I ran the shop. Lin does bookkeeping for a few local businesses, so we manage. Nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your share portfolio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, maybe five thousand dollars, in a few miners and a robotics company. I research them with the AI at night, and I check the boring numbers myself. Lin calls it my hobby, and she's right, it's not a retirement plan.

S0.say: I'd say the market has decided AI is a useful tool and not a miracle. He'd post a short note on a business forum and keep grading.
S0.think: He'd be a bit disappointed, having half planned around the tools, but a steady run to retirement suits him and Lin.
S0.do: Keeps grading and learning, aiming to get the road crown right by next winter. Keeps using AI daily for work and his small share portfolio, and saves a few hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm, more of a shrug than anything.
S0.quote: Lin calls it my hobby, and she's right, it's not a retirement plan.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is a former shopkeeper who accepts losing his business to a chain store as the market at work. He uses AI every day and enjoys it, which is unusual for a traditional, older worker. He's honest that his savings and pension are small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how markets work: some jobs shrink, new ones grow, and people who learn get ahead. I'd tell the young ones to get an apprenticeship and learn the tools. I wouldn't want the government stepping in much beyond training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's an opening for me. A grader is a simple machine to automate, so my job's at risk, sure. But the mine will need people to set up and check the automated road crews, and I'm the one who already talks to the AI every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine about the automation team in the first month. I'd also look at a side business with my son, who's an electrician, installing and maintaining small robots for farms and businesses around town. I'd put two thousand of savings into tools and training for that in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. Like the first year of the shop when Dad let me run the paint counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior and still learning the grader. Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course it is. I'm not going to pretend I'm the best operator. But I ran a shop for twenty-five years, and the thing I learned is that the person who shows up eager gets the next job, not always the person who's best at the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lin think of the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want to see the numbers first. She did the shop's books, so she knows what it costs when I get excited. We'd sit at the kitchen table with the AI and a calculator and work it out.

S1.say: I'd say this is how markets work, and people who learn get ahead. He'd urge young people towards apprenticeships and wouldn't want government doing much beyond training.
S1.think: He sees an opening: his grader job is easy to automate, but the mine will need people to set up and check automated road crews. He already talks to AI every night.
S1.do: Asks about the mine's automation team in the first month. Plans a side business with his electrician son installing and maintaining small robots, putting two thousand of savings into tools and training.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like his first year at the shop.
S1.quote: The person who shows up eager gets the next job, not always the person who's best at the old one.
S1.fieldNote: Ben's free-market views and his love of technology fit together naturally. He sees both his job risk and his opportunity clearly. Lin acts as a sensible check on his enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should look after their own and help their neighbours, and the market will find new work for people. But I'd admit two years is too fast for any market to adjust. I'd say maybe the government needs to help with retraining, though I'd hate to see people living on handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd like. If AI and robots can do anything, my son's electrical work might not be safe either. I'd be fifty-nine or sixty with a few months' savings, a small super and a side business that might already be out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go to the mine about the automation team, because a year of that pay is a year of savings. I'd cut the share hobby and keep the money as cash. Lin and I would look at renting out the granny flat behind our house for some income, and I'd help my son pivot his business to whatever the robots can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the week the chain store opened and the till went quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like handouts. What would you do if one came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, but I'd want it tied to something, training or community work. I don't want my grandkids growing up thinking money just arrives. I suppose that's me being old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, we've both lost businesses before, me with the shop and you nearly with that bad contract. We'll do what we did then: cut costs, find the next thing and work hard. He'd say, Dad, you sound like Grandad.

S2.say: I'd say people should look after their own and the market will find new work, though two years is too fast to adjust. He'd accept government help with retraining but hate to see people living on handouts.
S2.think: It worries him more than he'd like, since even his son's electrical work might not be safe. He'd be about sixty with a few months' savings, a small pension and a side business that might be out of date.
S2.do: Still seeks a place on the automation team to bank a year of good pay. Cashes out the share hobby, rents out the granny flat and helps his son pivot to work robots can't do yet.
S2.feel: Anxious, like the week the chain store opened and the till went quiet.
S2.quote: Like the week the chain store opened and the till went quiet.
S2.fieldNote: Ben's market faith is shaken by the speed of the two-year picture, and he admits the market can't adjust that fast. He still acts quickly: automation team, cash, granny flat, helping his son. His view of handouts softens but stays tied to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the market and for families to adjust, if people are willing to work. I'd tell people to get practical skills and learn the AI tools now. I'd say the government should stick to training and keep taxes low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three. I think I'd do well: a few years on the automation team, a side business with my son, then retire. It's not comfortable, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the automation team in the first year and do a short course in robotics maintenance at the technical college, maybe eight hundred dollars. I'd build the side business slowly, a few jobs a month, and grow our savings to a year's worth by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in charge. It feels like planning a shop renovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side business actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up and maintain robots for small farms and businesses, the mowers and milking machines and warehouse arms. A big company won't drive two hours out of town for a small job. We would, and we'd charge fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd be reacting. Five, I can build something with my son that's still standing when I retire. That's the difference between a fire sale and a proper business.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for markets and families to adjust if people will work. He'd push people to learn practical skills and AI tools, and want government to stick to training and low taxes.
S3.think: At sixty-three by 2031, he thinks he'd do well with a few years on the automation team and a side business with his son before retiring. It's not comfortable, but manageable.
S3.do: Joins the automation team in the first year and takes an eight-hundred-dollar robotics maintenance course at the technical college. Builds a side business slowly and grows savings to a year's worth by 2030.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in charge, like planning a shop renovation.
S3.quote: A big company won't drive two hours out of town for a small job. We would, and we'd charge fair.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Ben's small-business instincts take over and he plans a real business with his son. He sees a niche in rural robot maintenance that big firms will ignore. His views on government stay consistent: training yes, handouts no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people who use it will be fine. I'd tell young people to get trades and learn the tools. I'd say families and communities can handle most of it if government stays out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's good. I'd be sixty-eight and retired, after a few interesting years. I might even have a business to pass to my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading and learning, join the automation team when it comes and build the side business over five or six years. I'd keep saving and investing a bit. And I'd talk to my grandkids about careers that use their hands and the tools together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandkids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what my father told me in the shop: learn every tool on the shelf. These days the tools just happen to think. If you can use them and you're willing to work, you'll be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether people get lazy with the warning. Ten years is long enough for folks to tell themselves it's not real. I saw shopkeepers do that with the chain store, and they all closed the same year.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and people who use it will be fine. Families and communities can handle most of it if government stays out of the way.
S4.think: For him it's good news: he'd be sixty-eight and retired after a few interesting years, and might have a business to pass to his son.
S4.do: Keeps grading and joins the automation team when it comes, building the side business over five or six years. Keeps saving and investing and talks to his grandchildren about careers that use hands and tools together.
S4.quote: These days the tools just happen to think.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ben is calm and hopeful and sees a business to pass on. His father's advice from the shop is his guiding idea. His only worry is people ignoring a long warning, as shopkeepers did with the chain store.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything. What would help is cheap, fast training at the technical college, and fewer rules so small businesses like ours can start up quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd go back and keep the shop if I could. I wouldn't. Losing it taught me to move before the till goes quiet, not after.

headlineQuote: Losing it taught me to move before the till goes quiet, not after.
portrait: Ben Chen is a fifty-eight-year-old former hardware shop owner who now runs a grader on the haul roads at a bauxite mine, after a chain store took his customers. He's a churchgoing free-marketeer who uses AI every night to learn the job and research his small share portfolio. He stays calm through the plateau and steady change, seeing a chance to join the automation team and start a robot maintenance business with his electrician son. AGI in two years makes him anxious because it leaves no time to build, but with five or ten years he plans a business to pass on.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because there would be no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast training at the technical college and fewer rules so small businesses can start up quickly.
